cells.tense: The cycle closes here and you are standing in the open doorway, still holding the pen.
cells.ask: Finish something small today and stop exactly there. Then sit with the finished thing for one minute and notice you are still here.
cells.core: You can tell this piece is finished. The training holds because you are not waiting for a drumroll to call it done — you touch it once more for the contact, not for the verdict, and you have already turned toward whatever wants to begin. That is a specific kind of steadiness: the same attention, now with an exit.\nNothing has to be squeezed out of this one to prove the practice worked. The next thing does not need to be a bigger version. You can hold the closed one lightly and still mean it, and the small light stays lit because it is not carrying the whole reason you do this.
cells.sheetLine: The work closes and you stand in the doorway, pen still in hand.
cells.verb: Integrating what was made and letting it go, opening to the next cycle
cells.place: A small daily practice kept lit by attention

cells.tense: You are bracing at the end of a finish line you drew before the work was anywhere near done.
cells.ask: Pick the piece you have been calling finished and do one honest hour on it as if it were new. No announcements, no new title, no telling anyone about it.
cells.core: You are running past the actual end to a version up ahead where it is already complete and admired, and you have been practicing toward that instead of the work. The excitement is doing the deciding now — each small advance looks like the last one, so things get named done before they are.\nThe cost is real. Arriving early means the thing you made is still wet, and you hold it out anyway. You feel the gap between the version you claimed and the version on the table, and it pushes you harder into the next one. The practice does not need a ceremony. It needs the pen moving past the moment you would ordinarily stop.
cells.sheetLine: You keep calling the work done before the work is done.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that closed behind you, listening for it to open again.
cells.ask: Open one old unfinished thing and put it down for good — file it, delete it, or say it is over out loud. Then start something new and do ten minutes of it today.
cells.core: When the practice is going well, endings are ordinary. A piece gets finished, you look at it once, and you set it down. The next thing starts the same week, usually smaller than the last, and the small light stays lit because it is not being asked to carry every open question at once. That is what a closed cycle buys you: room.\nWhat is happening instead is that finished things sit in the same pile as unfinished ones. Each project gets held as provisional, so nothing counts as closed, and you carry all of it in the same arms. The attention is still there, spread across every loose end at once.\nThat is why the well runs low. The way back is not to push more into the tired arm. It is to let one cycle actually end — put the old thing down, and the grip frees up for whatever is arriving next.
cells.sheetLine: Nothing gets to be finished, so everything stays open at once.
cells.verb: Integrating what was made and letting it go, opening to the next cycle

cells.tense: The pen is down and you are still in a room you are already writing, telling yourself you have not started.
cells.ask: Name one routine you run and call it finished when it ends. Say so in the room, once, and let the next thing begin without being promised.
cells.core: You move through the practice and you do not describe it as yours. The small daily work shapes you, the finished pieces shape other people, and it gets called just what happens — a schedule, a habit, something anyone would do. It is hard to tell which cycles have closed and which are still open, so both get treated the same.\nAlmost nothing is missing except the saying-so. The clearing has been happening without you noticing the release, and it feels like no event because you have not let it be one. Admitting a thing is over costs less than you think, and it makes room for what is already coming in.
cells.sheetLine: You are writing in the room and calling it doing nothing.

attempts.check: The record gives Completion as Integration and completion fixed on presence, but the unsupported leap is that the person's effort was ever pointed somewhere it could finish, or that they could tell practice from performance well enough to decide it's done. The reader's likely objection is that some cycles genuinely cannot close yet, that the material is not theirs to complete, so any ask here can read as dismissing real reasons. The ask still holds if that read is wrong, because stopping to touch the work is useful whether the block is internal or structural, and it costs nothing to be told it doesn't apply. The sentence serving the writer would be one that quietly praises the stopping as the wise act, which flatters the reading rather than the person.
